content: CD99 antigen, also referred to as MIC2 or single-chain type-1 glycoprotein, is a transmembrane protein that is extensively O-glycosylated. It is encoded by the CD99 gene in humans and has a molecular weight of 32 kDa. Unlike most genes located on the X chromosome, the CD99 gene does not undergo X inactivation. It was the first pseudoautosomal gene identified in humans. CD99 is expressed on all leukocytes, with the highest levels observed on thymocytes. It is thought to enhance T-cell adhesion and facilitate apoptosis in double-positive T cells. The protein is also present in endothelial cells and within the periodontium, including gingival fibroblasts and gingival epithelial cells. CD99 plays a role in cellular migration and activation. Experimental studies suggest that it interacts with cyclophilin A. CD99 is expressed on the surface of Ewing's sarcoma tumors and is also detected in granulosa cell tumors. Its expression is elevated in malignant gliomas compared to normal brain tissue, and this overexpression is associated with increased tumor invasiveness and reduced survival rates. Antibodies targeting CD99 are utilized in diagnostic immunohistochemistry to differentiate Ewing's sarcoma from other histologically similar tumors. These antibodies are also used to identify thymic tumors and spindle cell tumors, such as synovial sarcoma, hemangiopericytoma, and meningioma. The EWS/FLI fusion protein is believed to regulate CD99 expression, but silencing EWS/FLI only modestly reduces CD99 levels. When CD99 expression is knocked down in human Ewing's sarcoma cells and these cells are transplanted into mice, the development of tumors and bone metastases is significantly reduced. Suppressing CD99 expression leads to increased β-III tubulin levels and enhanced neurite outgrowth. Conversely, upregulating CD99 expression in the L428 cell line, derived from Hodgkin's lymphoma, induces redifferentiation of these cells toward a B-cell phenotype. This suggests that the loss of B-cell differentiation in Hodgkin's lymphoma may be linked to CD99 downregulation. Interestingly, men appear to express higher levels of CD99 than women. In terms of prognostic significance, CD99 expression has been studied in various cancers. In patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the germinal center B-cell (GCB) subtype, positive CD99 expression is associated with improved 2-year event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS) compared to those with negative CD99 expression. However, in DLBCL patients with the non-GCB subtype, negative CD99 expression correlates with better 2-year EFS and OS. In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), higher CD99 expression in the stromal tissue is linked to a more favorable prognosis. CD99 also appears to influence cell-extracellular matrix interactions. By suppressing β1 integrin affinity, CD99 inhibits adhesion between cells and the extracellular matrix.
